source.title: A foundation model for the Earth system
source.authors: Cristian Bodnar; W. Bruinsma; Ana Lucic; Megan Stanley; Anna Allen; J. Brandstetter; P. Garvan; Maik Riechert; J. Weyn; Hai-Yu Dong; Jayesh K. Gupta; Kit Thambiratnam; Alexander T. Archibald; Chun-Chieh Wu; E. Heider; Max Welling; R. E. Turner; P. Perdikaris

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports parameter-scaling results for an Earth-system forecasting model, a different modality and training task from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Aurora validation loss scaling with parameter count at a fixed GPU-hour budget, and separately reports gains from adding diverse pretraining datasets. It does not test language-model cross-entropy, token-count scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or large-run extrapolation. Its references to the original scaling-law papers are citations, not results from those studies.
record.test_reason: Aurora, an Earth-system forecasting transformer, reports pretraining validation loss (weighted MAE) following a power law in parameter count, L(N) ∝ N^-0.026 at 5,000 GPU hours. This is a direct result on whether the power-law form carries over to a non-text modality (V5). It reports no language-model cross-entropy, token or compute-optimal sweeps, extrapolation, shape ablations or downstream-vs-scale fits.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that more diverse pretraining data and larger models improve validation performance (about 6% per tenfold size increase). They say no performance ceiling has been hit, and further scaling should improve fine-tuning results.
record.recipe_differences: This is an Earth-system forecasting model evaluated on validation loss, not a language model evaluated on held-out next-token cross-entropy. The reported size comparison fixes compute at 5,000 GPU hours; it does not fit the original language-model scaling setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that adding more diverse pretraining datasets improves validation performance; it does not report sensitivity of the fitted parameter exponent to fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding more diverse pretraining datasets (C1→C4) systematically improves validation RMSE, including on extreme values.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Earth-system foundation models, pretraining data diversity improves validation performance.

record.problems: The relevant scaling results are reported in figure captions without model sizes or uncertainty estimates for the fitted exponent. The study tests a weather-forecasting validation loss, not language-model cross-entropy.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results directly test a claim version. Comparisons of Aurora with operational forecasting systems and gains from fine-tuning are not power-law scaling results.

missing.what: The model sizes, number of models and parameter range of the scaling sweep, plus any fit uncertainty, needed to judge whether the power law spans several orders of magnitude.
missing.locator: Supplementary Information Section G; Extended Data Figs. 1c and 2 (plots)

record.verdict_notes: Aurora is not an original source, so a verdict is allowed. The paper notes that training is bottlenecked by data loading, so the fixed-GPU-hour comparison is not a clean compute-optimal setup. The exponent 0.026 is much smaller than Kaplan's language-model exponents, but V5 claims only the power-law form, not its exponent.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens or compute.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger from fits on small runs.
The loss-minimising parameter/token allocation as a function of compute.
Effects of depth, width or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study tests parameter-count scaling in one Earth-system forecasting setting, not other modalities or training regimes such as image/video generation, repeated data, fine-tuning or transfer.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices, or whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Aurora models of varying size
rows.size_stated: Aurora is described as a 1.3-billion-parameter model; sizes in the scaling sweep are not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Compared model parameter counts at a fixed amount of training compute.
rows.value: L(N) ∝ N−0.026 at 5,000 GPU hours; approximately 6% reduction in validation loss for every ten times increase in model size.
rows.note: The result is stated for the Earth-system forecasting model; it is not language-model cross-entropy.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The loss is the weighted-MAE pretraining objective on IFS HRES validation, not cross-entropy. The model sizes in the sweep, the number of models and the span of N are not given in the supplied text (they are in Supplementary Section G). So it cannot be confirmed that the fit spans several orders of magnitude. The main text paraphrases the same result as 'validation performance improves by approximately 6%'.

rows.subject: Aurora models of varying size
rows.size_stated: not stated for the models in the curves.
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation curves across parameter counts for surface-level variables.
rows.value: For every surface-level variable, validation loss roughly behaves as f(N) ∝ N−α, where α > 0 is an estimated parameter.
rows.note: The caption gives an aggregate statement across surface-level variables; individual variable names and exponent values are not provided in the supplied text.
rows.check: Per-variable fits are stated only qualitatively ('roughly behaves like'), with no exponents in the supplied text. The state could arguably be read as a weaker form of the same observation; it is kept as observed.

rows.subject: Aurora models pretrained with dataset configurations C1–C4
rows.operation_detail: Added increasingly diverse pretraining datasets and compared validation performance.
rows.value: Adding more diverse datasets systematically improves validation performance; the paper says improvements are especially apparent for extreme values.
rows.locator: Main text, Aurora section; Extended Data Fig. 1a–b caption
rows.note: This reports an effect of dataset diversity, not a power law in token count.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. Configurations C1–C4 vary dataset diversity, not token count along a power law, so the row does not measure any version's effect.

relationships.condition: Aurora Earth-system pretraining, validation loss vs parameter count at 5,000 GPU hours
relationships.reason: Validation loss fits L(N) ∝ N^-0.026 overall (R1) and roughly a power law for every surface variable (R2). The exponent is small, and the size range and fit quality are not reported in the main text.
relationships.display_finding: Overall validation loss fitted L(N)∝N^−0.026 and each surface variable showed approximate power-law scaling, without reported size range or fit quality.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
